newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Englishwoman breaks down at Cyprus assault trial.
newsitem.headline: Englishwoman breaks down at Cyprus assault trial.

text.p: An Englishwoman broke down in a Cyprus court on Monday after suggestions that she and her boyfriend provoked an attack by British soldiers charged with assaulting them and another friend.
Nursery nurse Claire Harbour, 22, burst into sobs during a defence lawyer's cross-examination about the attack by off-duty servicemen at a Cyprus coastal resort on August 2.

Roger Bell, 26, Tim Carter, 20, Steven Wolstencroft, 26, Steven Girvan, 20, and Stuart Spencer, 20, face charges of causing actual bodily harm to Harbour and grievous bodily harm to her boyfriend Barry Ford and another holidaymaker, Shane Bell, both 23.

The soldiers, from the British base at Dhekelia in southwest Cyprus, have pleaded not guilty to the charges, which carry maximum sentences of up to three years in prison. Shane Bell and Roger Bell are not related.
Ford, a quantity surveyor, suffered a shattered wrist.
Shane Bell, a car mechanic, needed surgery on a fractured jawbone.

Harbour, cross-examined for over two hours by Roger Bell's Cypriot defence counsel, stuck to her claim that the soldier attacked them outside a nightclub in the Ayia Napa resort and was joined by about eight more men.

"He assaulted me by pulling my hair, holding me and making me watch while my boyfriend was being kicked and punched...telling me not to worry and that it would all be over in a minute," Harbour sobbed.

Defence lawyer Tasos Katsikides apologised for upsetting her, but persisted with his line that she and Ford had provoked the argument. The lawyer claimed they had filed a complaint with police to sue for compensation, a charge Harbour denied. The hearing continues on Tuesday.
All three tourists are suing the five Britons for damages for a joint sum of up to 25,000 Cyprus pounds ($45,000).
The accused are members of the 600-strong Kings Regiment based at Dhekelia.
Immediately after the attack, the British bases banned visits to Ayia Napa by members of the regiment, just one month after an earlier ban was lifted.

The restrictions were first imposed in September 1994 after the brutal killing of a Danish tour guide by three members of the Royal Greenjackets regiment. They are serving a life sentence in Cyprus's central prison.
Some 3,500 troops are stationed at two military bases Britain has retained in Cyprus since independence in 1960.
